XpqqjU7u5Yc.context: Released in September 1977 by RSO Records, 'How Deep Is Your Love' was written and recorded as part of the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack, after producer Robert Stigwood requested songs from the Bee Gees for the film. The single topped the US Billboard Hot 100 on Christmas Eve 1977 — becoming the first of six consecutive American number-one hits — and stayed in the Top 10 for 17 weeks, a record at the time. It won Best Pop Performance by a Group at the 20th Grammy Awards (February 1978) and received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Original Song. The song marked the Bee Gees' transition from a pop-rock act to the defining voices of the disco era, while critics noted the track retained the melodic and harmonic sensibilities of their late-1960s ballad work. Barry Gibb has called it his favourite Bee Gees song, and in a 2011 ITV poll it was voted The Nation's Favourite Bee Gees Song by UK viewers.
XpqqjU7u5Yc.curatorial: An exceptionally high-value archival document capturing the Bee Gees at their commercial and artistic peak, directed by one of the founding figures of the music video form. Bruce Gowers' visual restraint — long takes, warm darkness, minimal motion — creates a document of the song's emotional weight rather than spectacle. As one of two known promotional versions of this single and a pre-MTV promo tied directly to a landmark cultural event (Saturday Night Fever), this clip is irreplaceable for researchers studying the transition between the broadcast promo era and the MTV video age.
XpqqjU7u5Yc.sig: A cornerstone of the soft-disco ballad genre, 'How Deep Is Your Love' demonstrated that the disco era could accommodate introspective, harmony-driven pop alongside floor-filling uptempo tracks. Its commercial success — ranking on Billboard's All Time Top 100 and Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs — helped establish the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack as one of the best-selling albums of all time, fundamentally shaping the late-1970s mainstream pop landscape. The promotional video, directed by Bruce Gowers, represents the pre-MTV promo clip tradition at its most refined: performance-first, aesthetically restrained, and built for broadcast.
XpqqjU7u5Yc.era: Late Disco / Soft Pop Golden Era (1977) - Peak Saturday Night Fever cultural moment; Bee Gees at the apex of their commercial dominance, blending ballad craftsmanship with disco-era production aesthetics
XpqqjU7u5Yc.movement: Disco / Soft Pop crossover — Saturday Night Fever cultural epoch (1977–1978)
XpqqjU7u5Yc.dbio: Bruce Gowers (21 Dec 1940 – 15 Jan 2023) was a Scottish-born British television director and producer. He trained at the BBC Training College and began his career as a cable puller, cameraman, and production manager before moving into directing. His 1975 music video for Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody' brought him international recognition and led to his relocation to the United States in the late 1970s. Over a career spanning more than four decades, Gowers directed approximately 350–500 music videos and helmed major live television productions including nine seasons of American Idol, winning an Emmy Award in 2009.

ih4JqI44Qz8.context: Chiquitita (Spanish version, 1979) sits at a unique intersection of pop diplomacy, UNICEF charity culture, and ABBA's deliberate push into the Latin American market. The English version debuted at the Music for UNICEF Concert at the UN General Assembly on 9 January 1979, with ABBA donating 50% of royalties to UNICEF. The Spanish version — lyrics by Buddy and Mary McCluskey — was released in Argentina in April 1979 and sold over 500,000 copies there within months, described as the biggest hit in South America in 25 years. The promo clip for the Spanish version served the concurrent Spanish and Latin American promotional campaign, appearing in the context of ABBA's broader strategy of recording Spanish-language material that would eventually produce the Gracias Por La Música album (1980). The video's slow, intimate visual approach mirrors the ballad's emotional register and the group's pivot away from disco spectacle toward sincere, cross-cultural accessibility.
ih4JqI44Qz8.curatorial: High. This Spanish-language promo represents a historically significant artefact of ABBA's Latin American breakthrough campaign, the UNICEF charity-pop moment of 1979, and the embryonic language of the pre-MTV performance promo clip in European pop. Its extreme editorial stillness (3 cuts, 324s) and warm desaturated palette are technically distinctive and culturally legible as late-1970s BBC-adjacent production values. Essential for any archive documenting multilingual pop marketing history or ABBA's visual catalogue.
ih4JqI44Qz8.sig: Represents a critical node in Europop's history as a cross-language export phenomenon. The Spanish Chiquitita promo is one of the earliest examples of a major European act producing a dedicated foreign-language music video to support a non-English single, anticipating the multilingual marketing strategies that would become standard in global pop decades later. Its low-motion, performance-locked visual grammar defines the ABBA promo aesthetic of intimate balladry distinct from the group's more elaborate disco-era clips.

ZhIsAZO5gl0.context: Released in 1979 as the lead single from Kiss's seventh studio album Dynasty, 'I Was Made for Lovin' You' represented a calculated and controversial pivot toward disco-influenced pop for one of hard rock's most iconographic bands. The song was co-written by Paul Stanley with Desmond Child and Vini Poncia — marking Kiss's first outside songwriting collaboration with Child, who would later pen hits for Bon Jovi, Aerosmith, and Ricky Martin. The track drew accusations of sellout from the Kiss Army, yet became the band's biggest commercial crossover, reaching No. 11 on the US Billboard chart, No. 1 in France and the Netherlands, and eventually surpassing one billion YouTube views. The promotional video — shot on the Dynasty tour stage in a cancelled-show scenario — embodies the pre-MTV era's pragmatic approach to music video: a performance document with minimal production embellishment, relying entirely on the band's theatrical visual identity to carry the clip.
ZhIsAZO5gl0.curatorial: Exceptionally high. This is one of the most-viewed pre-MTV music videos in existence, with over one billion YouTube views as of early 2026. It is a primary archival document of the disco-rock crossover moment, the Kiss theatrical aesthetic at its Dynasty-era peak, and the pre-MTV performance clip format. Its quantitative metrics — extreme slow editing, high saturation, low brightness — are a near-textbook fingerprint of 1979 arena-stage promotional filming. Essential for any study of late-1970s rock commercialization, music video history, or theatrical rock identity.
ZhIsAZO5gl0.sig: A landmark document of late-1970s disco-rock hybridity, this video captures Kiss at the commercial apex of their classic-era persona while the genre itself stood at a cultural crossroads. The performance-only format, shot on an extant arena stage, is a direct artifact of the pre-MTV promotional clip economy. The song and its video helped legitimize outside co-writing in hard rock and influenced a generation of crossover singles production.

C-TSvxZ40RQ.context: Released in August 1982 alongside the album 'Rock in a Hard Place' on Columbia Records, this video arrives at a pivotal and turbulent moment for Aerosmith. It is the band's only charting song from the lineup without guitarist Joe Perry, who had departed in 1979 and been replaced by Jimmy Crespo. Guitarist Brad Whitford also departed after recording his parts. The video's gang-fight street narrative taps directly into the urban threat aesthetic popularized by films like 'The Warriors' (1979), translating that cinematic language into the nascent music video format. Aerosmith's decision to produce one of their first genuine music videos for MTV signals the industry's recognition of the channel—launched just one year prior in August 1981—as a critical promotional platform. The dark, sepia-toned street aesthetic and rapid cutting reflect both the band's hardened blues-rock identity and the broader hard rock genre's visual vocabulary at the dawn of the video age.
C-TSvxZ40RQ.curatorial: High curatorial value as a primary document of both Aerosmith's turbulent early-1980s period and the inaugural generation of MTV music videos. The video preserves a transitional moment in rock history—a classic band adapting to a new medium with a lineup in flux—while Arnold Levine's direction exemplifies the formal vocabulary of the era. The dark cinematography, gang narrative, and rapid intercutting make it an essential reference point for the pre-hair-metal hard rock visual canon.
C-TSvxZ40RQ.sig: A historically significant artifact as one of Aerosmith's first deliberately produced music videos for MTV broadcast. The song reached #21 on the U.S. Mainstream Rock Tracks chart and stands as the sole charting Aerosmith single from the Perry-absent lineup. It demonstrates how established hard rock acts adapted to the emerging video medium by fusing performance footage with narrative gang imagery, establishing a template for the genre's visual language in the early 1980s.
C-TSvxZ40RQ.era: Early MTV Era (1982) - One of Aerosmith's first purpose-built music videos, produced during the transitional dawn of the music video medium and the band's turbulent lineup-change period.

B7Z-eUmR2bM.context: Released in July 1985 as the third single from 'No Jacket Required,' 'Don't Lose My Number' arrived during Phil Collins' unparalleled commercial peak. The video is a direct product of — and commentary on — the MTV industrial complex at its mid-decade zenith. VH1 had launched just weeks after 'No Jacket Required' was released, and Collins was, as Rolling Stone described, its de facto patron saint. By parodying the visual languages of The Police, The Cars, David Lee Roth, and Elton John within a single clip, Yukich and Collins produced one of the era's most self-aware documents: a video explicitly about the anxiety and absurdity of making music videos. The piece functions simultaneously as a commercial product and a critique of that product, presaging the self-referential media culture of the following decade. The 2025 HD remaster was released under the '#NoJacketRequired40' campaign, signaling institutional recognition of the video's archival and cultural value.
B7Z-eUmR2bM.curatorial: Exceptionally high. This video is a primary-source document of mid-80s MTV culture that functions simultaneously as entertainment, industry self-critique, and a compressed visual encyclopedia of the era's dominant music video aesthetics. Its confirmed director, well-documented production context, and recent HD remaster make it an ideal anchor artifact for any archive covering 1983–1987 mainstream pop-rock visual culture. The meta-comedy structure gives it pedagogical utility far beyond standard performance or narrative videos of the period.
B7Z-eUmR2bM.sig: A landmark in the 'meta-music video' sub-genre, 'Don't Lose My Number' is one of the earliest and most accomplished examples of a major pop artist explicitly foregrounding the artificiality of the video form. Its sketch-comedy structure and genre-parody vignettes influenced subsequent self-aware video productions and document the dense intertextual visual culture of peak MTV. The video also showcases the breadth of mid-80s pop-rock visual iconography in a single compressed artifact.
B7Z-eUmR2bM.era: Mid-Decade MTV Golden Age (1985) - Peak of the music video format as mainstream entertainment; Phil Collins at the commercial apex of his solo career during the 'No Jacket Required' era.

SXODGahChBM.context: Released in September 1987 by Camouflage, a synth-pop trio from Bietigheim-Bissingen, West Germany, 'The Great Commandment' emerged at the intersection of Cold War European youth anxiety and the global expansion of electronic club culture. The single crossed from European charts (peaking at #14 in Germany and Top 10 in over 20 countries) into the U.S. Billboard Dance Club Songs chart, where it reached #1 for three non-consecutive weeks, an exceptional feat for a West German debut act. Its MTV rotation amplified Camouflage's transatlantic reach and positioned them alongside Depeche Mode and Kraftwerk in the global electronic pop consciousness.

SXODGahChBM.sig: A landmark artifact of late-1980s West German synth-pop, 'The Great Commandment' bridged Kraftwerk's machine-electronic precision with Depeche Mode's gothic anti-establishment ethos. As Camouflage's debut single, it demonstrated that European electronic acts could achieve Billboard Dance #1 status in the U.S. market, opening pathways for subsequent cross-Atlantic synth-pop crossovers. TNNpQM9TY84.context: Released in July 1987 as the lead single from Babylon and On, 'Hourglass' arrived at a moment when MTV's rotational power could transform a niche British band into a US chart contender overnight. Squeeze had long been celebrated in the UK but struggled to convert critical acclaim into American sales. The Edmondson-directed video — suffused with Dalí-esque optical illusions and practical forced-perspective effects — became a perfect vehicle for MTV's appetite for visually arresting concept videos. The decision to hire Adrian Edmondson, a comedian-director from the British alternative comedy scene rather than a conventional promo director, reflects the cross-pollination between UK TV's anarchic visual culture and the music video industry in 1987. The video's MTV VMA win for Best Special Effects in 1988 placed it in a prestigious lineage alongside a-ha's 'Take On Me' (1986) and Peter Gabriel's 'Sledgehammer' (1987), cementing it as a landmark of practical-effects artistry in the pre-CGI era.
TNNpQM9TY84.curatorial: Tier-1 archival priority. 'Hourglass' is a historically verified MTV VMA-winning music video representing the apex of analogue, practical-effects surrealism in British pop video production. Its cultural significance is multi-layered: it is simultaneously Squeeze's commercial breakthrough in the US, a landmark in pre-CGI visual effects craft, and an artefact of the fertile cross-pollination between 1980s British alternative comedy and the music video industry. Its warm-toned, high-contrast, film-shot aesthetic is a textbook signature of late-80s A&M Records production values and merits permanent preservation as a primary document of the MTV Golden Age.
TNNpQM9TY84.sig: A defining example of British New Wave's late-period US breakthrough, 'Hourglass' demonstrates how a high-concept, effects-driven music video could overcome a band's perceived regional specificity and drive mainstream chart success. Its win at the 1988 MTV VMAs for Best Special Effects canonises it as one of the premier practical-effects videos of the analogue era, predating CGI dominance and showcasing the creative peak of in-camera surrealist technique in pop music video production.

Min5jvGu9sQ.context: Released in late 1993 as a single from the album Thirteen, 'Hang On' emerged during a pivotal transitional moment for Teenage Fanclub—following the surprise North American success of Bandwagonesque (1991) and amid the global dominance of Seattle grunge. Creation Records, as the home label for UK release, positioned the band within the premier British indie infrastructure of the era. The video's direction by a then-emerging Spike Jonze connects the Scottish indie scene to the American skate-culture and youth-media underground that would define mid-90s alternative video aesthetics.

Min5jvGu9sQ.sig: Emblematic of the early-90s power-pop and jangle-pop revival, 'Hang On' demonstrates the melodic, harmony-driven songwriting that distinguished Teenage Fanclub from their grunge contemporaries. As the opening track of Thirteen, it anchors the album's ambition and serves as a document of the band's creative peak on Creation Records. The video's rapid editorial style, under Spike Jonze, prefigures the kinetic indie-rock clip aesthetic that would flourish through 1994-1996.

iqIq4B1rgl4.context: Released during the peak of mid-90s dancehall and reggae crossover into mainstream UK pop, 'Mysterious Girl' exemplifies a moment when Caribbean rhythmic influences saturated the British charts alongside acts such as Shaggy, Maxi Priest, and Chaka Demus & Pliers. Peter Andre, an Australian-born performer who had cultivated a teen idol following in the UK, used the video's exotic Thai location to project aspirational tropical escapism — a recurring trope in 90s pop visual culture. The video's body-centred, beach-resort aesthetic also intersected with the growing commercialisation of gym physique culture in pop media. The song was subsequently re-released in 2004 following Andre's appearance on the UK reality show I'm a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here!, where it reached number one on the UK Singles Chart — an unusual dual-era chart life that makes the video a documented artefact of both mid-90s pop-reggae and early-2000s reality TV pop revival.
iqIq4B1rgl4.curatorial: High curatorial value as a doubly significant pop artefact: a primary document of the 1995–96 UK pop-reggae crossover moment, and a secondary document of the 2004 reality-TV-driven nostalgia revival cycle. The confirmed Phi Phi Islands, Thailand location shoot, modest £30,000 budget, and Claudia Castle's direction represent a well-documented production chain for a video that reached number one on the UK Singles Chart. Its warm-saturated, beach-performance visual grammar is an immediately recognisable and historically locatable aesthetic marker, making it a strong teaching and exhibition resource for 90s popular culture studies.
iqIq4B1rgl4.sig: A canonical example of mid-90s UK pop-reggae crossover production. The video codified a specific tropical-escapism visual grammar — shirtless male lead, sun-bleached lagoon setting, dancehall-adjacent artist feature — that was widely replicated in the genre. Its fast-cut, MTV-formatted editing pace and warm-saturated palette defined affordable mid-tier UK pop promo aesthetics of 1995–1996. The song's dual chart success across two decades (1996 and 2004) gives it rare longitudinal cultural significance as both a primary artefact and a revival document.

Woo-UW9NZvc.context: That Was My Veil emerged from Dance Hall at Louse Point, the debut collaborative album between John Parish and PJ Harvey, released 23 September 1996 on Island Records. The project followed Harvey's commercial breakthrough To Bring You My Love (1995) and was regarded by Island Records as a potential 'commercial suicide' — an avant-garde detour that Harvey and Parish pursued deliberately. Parish wrote and performed all instruments; Harvey wrote the lyrics and sang. The collaboration underscored their deep creative bond stretching back to Harvey's teenage years playing in Parish's band Automatic Dlamini. Critics praised the album's 'brooding rural blues' and 'total immersion'; Rolling Stone called it 'incredible.' The video's December 1996 release coincided with a brief UK club tour with the Mark Bruce Dance Company, reinforcing the project's performance-art and experimental credentials.
Woo-UW9NZvc.curatorial: High curatorial value as a confirmed-director video from a critically significant and commercially anomalous 1996 collaboration. Represents the intersection of fine-art photography, lo-fi analogue film direction, and British alt-rock's experimental avant-garde. Fully restored for the 2020 vinyl reissue, conferring archival institutional endorsement. A key primary source for studying Mochnacz's visual authorship and PJ Harvey's mid-career artistic identity.
Woo-UW9NZvc.sig: Represents a pivotal document of mid-90s British alternative rock's experimental wing — a moment when a major-label artist (PJ Harvey) deliberately pursued avant-garde collaboration over commercial consolidation. The video's lo-fi, high-contrast fine-art aesthetic, helmed by Mochnacz, helped define the visual grammar of art-rock music video in the era, privileging authenticity and intensity over production sheen.
Woo-UW9NZvc.era: Mid-90s British Alternative Rock (1996) - Post-breakthrough collaborative period following PJ Harvey's To Bring You My Love; avant-garde label output on Island Records at peak of Britpop-adjacent art-rock experimentation
Woo-UW9NZvc.movement: British mid-90s art-rock / post-grunge avant-garde (alternative rock reinvention)
Woo-UW9NZvc.dbio: Maria Mochnacz is a British photographer and music video director, best known for her long-term creative collaboration with PJ Harvey. Trained in fine arts at Coventry Polytechnic (1983–1986) and subsequently in photography, she began working with musicians and bands from 1991. She directed the majority of PJ Harvey's music videos and contributed to album artwork and styling across Harvey's career. Her directorial credits include Dress (1991), Sheela Na Gig (1992), Man-Size (1993), Down by the Water (1995), and That Was My Veil (1996). She has also collaborated with Marianne Faithfull, Robert Plant, Nick Cave, Richard Ashcroft, M People, and Robert Miles. Her photographic style has been described as 'lo-fi but with a hard fine art edge.'

vBJtS3IhwCY.context: Released in 1996 as the lead single from Gone Again, 'Summer Cannibals' marked Patti Smith's return to recording after an eight-year absence defined by domestic life in Detroit and the 1994 death of her husband Fred 'Sonic' Smith. By enlisting Robert Frank — a titan of 20th-century documentary photography and a key figure in the Beat artistic milieu Smith inhabited in the 1970s — Smith anchored the video in the same anti-commercial, outsider art tradition as her greatest work. The video's rejection by MTV is itself culturally significant, marking a collision between Smith's uncompromising artistic identity and the glossy visual grammar of mid-90s mainstream music television.
vBJtS3IhwCY.curatorial: Exceptionally high. Its rejection by MTV and subsequent preservation in museum and online contexts make it a canonical example of art-world values clashing with commercial music television. The quantitative profile — muted, warm, low-contrast, slow-paced — is a perfect metric fingerprint of Frank's visual philosophy applied to the music video format. Tier 1 archival priority.
vBJtS3IhwCY.sig: Represents a pivotal artifact of mid-90s art-punk revival and the broader cultural reassertion of first-generation punk figures in the alternative rock mainstream. The Frank-directed video is a rare collision of canonical fine-art photography/filmmaking with the pop music video format, and stands as a document of New York's post-CBGB bohemian underground persisting against commercial pressures.

0S43IwBF0uM.context: Released at the cusp of the post-big beat transition, 'Star Guitar' arrived as The Chemical Brothers — and UK electronic music broadly — were moving away from the aggressive, sample-heavy sound of the late 1990s toward more melodic, house-influenced territory. It remains one of the most referenced examples of music-image synchronisation in contemporary music video scholarship, and represents a pivotal moment in The Chemical Brothers' evolution from big beat to progressive electronic production.

VcmfrMNPcKc.context: Released in 1985, 'Here Is My Number' is the debut single from Makin' Time, a West Midlands band signed to Countdown Records (distributed by Stiff Records) and central to the mid-1980s second wave of British mod revival. By this point the original late-1970s mod revival spearheaded by The Jam had subsided, but a cluster of bands — including Makin' Time, The Prisoners, and Secret Affair — sustained the subculture through small-label releases, all-dayer events, and fanzine culture. VcmfrMNPcKc.curatorial: High. This video is a documented artefact at the intersection of two historically significant trajectories: the mid-1980s British mod revival's second phase, and the very early directorial career of Nigel Dick — who would become one of the most influential music video directors of the late 20th century. As a rare low-budget performance promo confirmed on IMVDb, it offers a precise counterpoint to Dick's later high-production work and provides primary visual evidence of the Countdown/Stiff mod revival scene's promotional output. The band's subsequent legacy (Martin Blunt/The Charlatans) adds further archival weight.
VcmfrMNPcKc.sig: One of the most musically accomplished singles of the 1980s British mod revival second wave, 'Here Is My Number' demonstrates the genre's pivot from punk-influenced rawness to a cleaner power-pop and soul synthesis. As a debut single produced with a full marketing budget on a Stiff-affiliated imprint, it represents the commercial ambitions — and ultimate commercial frustrations — of the mid-80s mod scene. It also stands as an early music video credit for Nigel Dick, one of the most decorated music video directors in history.
VcmfrMNPcKc.era: Mid-1980s UK Mod Revival (1985) - Second-wave mod revival period; West Midlands indie bands operating on Stiff-distributed independent labels, bridging 1960s soul-pop aesthetics with post-punk energy in the pre-Britpop landscape.
